 BUSINESS Minimum Wage Negotiations: Take Care of the Worker, but also the Employers
 Published: November 19, 2026 
 Share 
 SHARE 
 The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions of Bosnia and Herzegovina has proposed a new model for calculating minimum wage increases. For a worker with a primary school education, the minimum wage would be 1,500 KM, while for those with a university degree, it would be 1,900 KM. However, this proposal is unacceptable to both the government and employers. The minimum wage must be adjusted by the new year; however, given that the current government is on its way out and it is unclear when a new one will be formed, it appears that the deadlines will not be met. Economists, meanwhile, warn that any wage increase must take into account both the workers and the employers, noting that economic development in the Federation is currently in decline.
 While employees are taking to the streets to demand higher wages, the Trade Union insists that solutions exist. Their proposal involves linking regular wage adjustments to the growth of the average wage, while also tailoring the minimum wage to the worker’s level of education.
 SAMIR KURTOVIĆ, President of the Confederation of Independent Trade Unions of BiH
 “We will see what happens with this government and what happens with the new one. If we run into problems, we will certainly organize protests in front of the Federation of BiH Government and the Employers’ Association.”
 The most recent meeting of the Economic and Social Council yielded no results. The Trade Union points out that while the government is offering a 3.5 percent wage increase, the cost of the “consumer basket” (the basic cost of living) has risen by 9 percent. Furthermore, they point out that only 4.46 percent of employers have paid the non-taxable portion of the 300 KM aid to their workers, even though employer-borne social security contributions in the Federation have been reduced by 5 percent. The Government, it seems, is not backing down from its position.
 AMIR HASIČEVIĆ, Minister of Trade of the FBiH
 “I believe that, ultimately, this will come down to the adjustment of wages, rather than the 1,500 or 1,900 [KM] thresholds that were originally envisioned in the scales.”
 Economists who are also members of the legislative branch emphasize the need for further reform of the tax system. This entails lowering the aggregate social security contribution rate from 36 to 31 percent and shifting the focus toward the average wage, rather than the minimum wage.
 ADMIR ČAVALIĆ, economist and member of the FBiH Parliament
 “It is more realistic to expect that this problem will only be addressed next year—specifically, when the issues of lowering the aggregate social contribution rate, reforming the labor market, and implementing an online fiscalization model are brought to the table.”
 Economist Željko Rička notes that the current moment is unfavorable for advocating for better living standards for workers, given high inflation and a decline in industrial production.
 ŽELJKO RIČKA, professor of economics
 “Prices are rising—a trend beyond our control, as policies set in other countries directly impact our resources. On the other hand, the decline in industrial production is our own fault. You cannot expect higher earnings while industrial output is falling; the two simply do not go together.”
 Most economic experts agree that a new model for wage increases must be found, but they also warn that shifting the entire burden of such increases onto employers is dangerous.
 EDIN GLOGIĆ, professor of economics
 “While it is certainly not a solution for workers to earn low wages, it is equally problematic if the economy collapses—as the economy is the engine that keeps a state functioning. If economic activity falls short of where it should be, we will all face long-term difficulties. Ultimately, this underscores that reform must be the top priority.”
 As a mutually acceptable method for raising wages is sought, the incumbent authorities are announcing hikes in electricity and gas prices—increases likely to drive up the cost of essential goods. Consequently, inflation is poised to ‘eat up’ any wage increases, regardless of their size.
